name: International Maritime Organization: The MASS Code for Autonomous Shipping
title: International Maritime Organization: The MASS Code for Autonomous Shipping
answer: The International Maritime Organization, the United Nations agency that writes international shipping rules, publishes an FAQ on autonomous shipping and the International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships. The most useful fact for anyone following AI in transport is that the non-mandatory MASS Code was adopted in May 2026 and took effect on 1 July 2026, creating a goal-based safety framework for autonomous and remotely operated cargo ships, with the master retaining overall responsibility even when not on board.

sections.body: The source is the website of the International Maritime Organization, the body that sets international rules for shipping. The substantive material sits on an FAQ page about autonomous shipping and the International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships, known as the MASS Code, supported by pages describing IMO events on the same subject. The FAQ explains what the Code is, when it was adopted and when it took effect, which ships it covers and what it requires. The event pages record a symposium co-organised with the Government of Norway in June 2025 and a seminar for ports and public authorities in April 2024.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The MASS Code was adopted by the Maritime Safety Committee in May 2026 by resolution MSC.595(111) and came into effect on 1 July 2026. It is non-mandatory, and Member States are encouraged to apply it and to share their experience through the MASS Experience-Building Phase. The Code establishes a goal-based framework intended to ensure that autonomous ships are designed, constructed, operated and certified to safety and environmental standards equivalent to conventional ships. It applies to cargo ships covered under SOLAS Chapter I, generally ships over 500 gross tonnage on international voyages, and Member States are recommended to apply it as far as practicable to ships below that threshold. A MASS is defined as a ship which, to a varying degree, can operate independently of human interaction, and only when autonomous or remote technologies replace or support functions normally carried out by crew on board. Enhanced automation alone does not make a ship a MASS, and such ships gain no privileges over conventional vessels. To qualify, a ship must complete the approval process and hold a valid MASS Safety Certificate. The Code requires a description of the modes of operation for which a ship is designed, risk assessment by operators, and defined operating limits covering wind speed, sea state, visibility, water depth, adverse weather and day or night operation, together with the actions to be taken when conditions move outside those limits. Human oversight is underscored, with the master retaining overall responsibility at all times even if not on board, including through Remote Operations Centres where trained personnel monitor or control vessel functions from ashore.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives the adoption of the MASS Code in May 2026 by resolution MSC.595(111), its entry into effect on 1 July 2026, and its application to cargo ships generally over 500 gross tonnage on international voyages under SOLAS Chapter I. It defines a MASS as a ship able to operate independently of human interaction to a varying degree, and states that a valid MASS Safety Certificate is required for a ship to qualify. It records the MASS symposium held on 17 June 2025 in London, co-organised with Norway, and the ports seminar held on 11 April 2024.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in transport, this is the primary source for the international rules now shaping autonomous navigation, collision avoidance and crewless operation at sea. It sets out the regulatory baseline that ship designers, operators and technology suppliers must work to, including the requirement to define operating conditions and limits and to manage risk across a vessel's operation. It also makes clear where responsibility sits, with the master accountable even when ashore, and it names Remote Operations Centres as the shore-side model for monitoring and control. The event pages show how ports and public authorities are being brought into preparation for autonomous ships arriving in their waters.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Transportation

sections.body: The MASS Code described here is non-mandatory, so its application depends on Member States, and the text does not set out enforcement or penalties. The FAQ is a summary rather than the full text of the Code, and it does not detail the technical standards for AI navigation or collision avoidance systems themselves. Coverage is limited to cargo ships under SOLAS Chapter I, with smaller vessels only recommended for inclusion. The event pages are records of past gatherings rather than findings, and the material is dated to the period of adoption in 2026.
